articles.title: How Colombia’s outgoing president protected 42% of the country’s Amazon from mining
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM On August 4, 2026, three days before he left office, Colombian President Gustavo Petro signed a resolution placing 186,500 square miles of the Amazon off-limits to any new extraction. That means no new mining concessions, no new oil or gas contracts, and no environmental permits that would make either […]
The post How Colombia’s outgoing president protected 42% of the country’s Amazon from mining first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

On August 4, 2026, three days before he left office, Colombian President Gustavo Petro signed a resolution placing 186,500 square miles of the Amazon off-limits to any new extraction. That means no new mining concessions, no new oil or gas contracts, and no environmental permits that would make either possible. The deadline was not incidental. Petro’s successor had campaigned on reviving oil exploration and legalizing fracking.

What made this move unusual was the legal mechanism. The government reached back more than 50 years to invoke Article 47 of the Natural Resources Code, a statute that allows the Colombian state to exclude an entire region from private exploitation rights. It had been used before, in smaller pieces, but never applied to the whole Colombian Amazon at once.

What the resolution does and doesn’t do

This is not a national park. It does not fit any existing legal conservation category. What it does, specifically, is prohibit three things: issuing new mining concessions, signing new oil or gas contracts, and granting the environmental permits that accompany either.

Before the resolution was signed, there were 164 active mining titles, 284 pending applications, and 39 active oil and gas contracts; since they are existing operations, they can’t be touched. All of those continue until their contracts expire, but fortunately, what is off limits for them is a renewal. The effect is not an immediate halt but a permanent door closing on anything new.

One narrow exception applies: small-scale extraction of construction materials for local road repair remains allowed, though even that is off-limits within indigenous territories.

The incoming administration

Abelardo de la Espriella took office on August 7, four days after the resolution was signed. During his campaign, he pledged to revive oil exploration and legalize hydraulic fracturing nationwide, describing the practice as modern and responsible. His incoming environment minister has already signaled that fracking will proceed in certain areas.

The new government has not commented on the Amazon reserve specifically, however that silence may not last. Because this is an administrative resolution rather than a law, it is more vulnerable to reversal than legislation would be.

Why the Ministry says this is urgent

The deforestation data the Ministry of Environment cited makes a clear case. Between 2016 and 2023, the Colombian Amazon lost 1.95 million acres of forest, accounting for 60% of all deforestation recorded across the country during that period. Between 2022 and 2024 alone, another 645,000 acres disappeared.

The technical diagnosis points to what specialists call the fishbone effect. When a road is cut to service an extractive project, it branches into side roads that gradually open territory to settlement, illegal logging, and illicit crops far beyond the area originally permitted. The road is not just a road. It is an entry point.

The resolution also rests on a legal foundation that has been building for years. In 2018, Colombia’s Supreme Court recognized the Colombian Amazon as a subject of rights, effectively giving the rainforest legal standing to be protected in its own right. In 2025, the Constitutional Court reinforced that precedent by designating it a specially protected ecosystem.

What indigenous communities cover

Of the total protected area, 55%, or about 66.2 million acres, consists of indigenous reserves. One figure from that land is worth stating plainly: indigenous territories in the Colombian Amazon retain 99.5% of their forest cover intact and hold approximately 78% of all the carbon stored in the region.

Where indigenous communities manage the land, the forest fares better than anywhere else. That is not simply a talking point, there is recorded evidence to support this.

Before signing the resolution, the government consulted the region’s indigenous peoples at a meeting on July 19 and 20. Consultation with Afro-Colombian, Raizal, and Palenquero communities had not yet concluded, so the resolution explicitly states it will not apply to their territories until that process is complete.

What is at stake for water and climate?

The Ministry’s central argument is not about biodiversity alone. It is about water. The Amazon’s roughly 400 billion trees release approximately 20 billion tons of water vapor into the atmosphere every day, a phenomenon researchers call flying rivers. Around 670 million people across Latin America depend on those invisible rivers, which supply much of the moisture that feeds rainfall in Colombia’s eastern mountain range and the high-altitude wetlands that supply Bogotá’s water.

The region also stores an estimated 6.5 gigatons of carbon. Researchers have flagged the risk of a tipping point from which the Amazon could not recover on its own, gradually transforming from rainforest into something resembling savanna. The consequences of that shift would extend well beyond Colombia’s borders.

Colombia is now the strictest of the eight nations that share the Amazon basin, which include Brazil, Peru, Ecuador, Bolivia, Venezuela, Guyana, and Suriname, in its commitment to keeping extraction out of its portion of the forest. Whether that commitment holds will depend entirely on a government that did not sign the measure but inherited it on its very first day in office.

articles.title: Wild dogs record 2,500-mile trek across Zambia in search of a mate
articles.summary: Scientists say the record-breaking journey by three brothers offers hope wildlife can survive growing pressures.
articles.content:
Three sisters almost completed an equally epic journey, but stopped when one became trapped in a snare.

African wild dogs are among Africa's rarest predators, with only about 6,000 remaining in the wild.

They live in highly social packs, hunt together and are known for their vast roaming in search of new territory and breeding opportunities with other packs.

They cannot breed within the pack they are born into, so they either wait and may eventually inherit their pack, or set off at the age of two or three in search of a mate.

The brothers covered about 260 miles in a straight line over the course of eight months, but travelled nearly 10 times that overall while crossing through a broken-up landscape.

These sorts of journeys are known as dispersals - travelling one way in search of a mate, which is a behaviour distinct from migrations, where animals move back and forth with the seasons in search of food or habitat.

The UN Convention on Migratory Species identifies Africa's longest migrations as wildebeest moving seasonally between Tanzania and Kenya in search of grazing and water covering more than 400 miles.

Globally, caribou undertake the longest single land migrations of any animal - travelling 839 miles in a round trip, while grey wolves have been recorded travelling more than 4,350 miles over a year.

Perhaps even more significant than the distance itself was the route the wild dogs took through Zambia.

They moved between wildlife strongholds, skirting areas containing major human obstacles, including the capital, Lusaka, and heavily developed industrial areas.

The findings suggest wild dog populations across eastern and southern Africa may remain more connected than conservationists previously believed.

Professor Scott Creel of Montana State University, the paper's lead author, who has been studying African wild dogs since 1991, said the study provides cautious optimism.

"It's plausible to believe that every major wild dog population in eastern and southern Africa, other than fenced ones, are potentially connected," he said.

But he said, in conservation,"the glass is half empty and the glass is half full", highlighting the threat of poaching snares.

While the three male wild dogs successfully completed their extraordinary journey, two of the three females died.

Researchers identified a pattern in which surviving pack members repeatedly returned to the same location, a behaviour that often signals the death of a companion.

The research, published in the journal, Ecology, external, adds weight to calls to create strips of natural land outside protected areas that connect separate wildlife areas broken apart by roads, towns, or farms.

Bruce Ellender, one of the paper's co-authors and Kafue Conservation director for the environmental charity, The Nature Conservancy, said species that roam over large areas, such as wild dogs and elephants, need connected landscapes if they are to survive into the future.

"We can't see these protected areas as islands and expect them to be functional in the long term, we need to think much broader than that," he said.

articles.title: A coral reef thought dead for 60 years is teeming with life
articles.summary: More than 60 years after surveys suggested a deep coral reef off Benin was probably dead, scientists have found it alive. Cameras revealed healthy-looking coral patches supporting multiple fish species more than 50 meters beneath the surface. The discovery suggests West Africa’s coastal waters may contain other overlooked reefs that have yet to be documented.
articles.content:
A coral reef off the coast of Benin that was thought to be dead for decades has been found alive and apparently healthy.

Surveys conducted in the 1960s, which were primarily designed to locate productive fishing grounds, identified what appeared to be a deep-water coral reef. At the time, researchers concluded that the reef was probably dead. More than 60 years later, scientists returned to the area armed with modern sonar and the Deep Sea Camera System provided by the National Geographic Exploration Technology Lab.

What they found was very different from what the historical records had suggested.

"It was not an easy field campaign," said Gérard Zinzindohoué of the Institut de Recherches Halieutiques et Océanologiques du Bénin, lead author of the article in Frontiers in Marine Science. "It was a mix of long days at sea, technical problems, and a lot of uncertainty. But then we saw structures on the sonar that looked like they could be reef signatures, which gave us hope that we were close.

"Next, we surveyed the structures with an underwater drone and the Deep Sea Camera System. That was a big moment for us, because suddenly we could actually see the seafloor. I still remember seeing those first images. It was a mix of excitement and disbelief, because after all this time thinking about this reef, suddenly there was something real in front of us."

A Deep Coral Ecosystem Thought To Be Dead

The older surveys had placed the possible reef more than 50 meters below the ocean surface and described it as probably dead. Zinzindohoué and his colleagues suspected that the site might instead contain a mesophotic coral ecosystem.

"A mesophotic coral ecosystem lives deeper than the usual shallow coral reefs, in zones where light is much more limited," explained Zinzindohoué. "Unlike typical shallow reefs, it does not always form a single continuous reef structure. Instead, it can appear as patchy or scattered coral communities spread across the seafloor."

Guided by the decades-old survey records, the researchers scanned 11.5 kilometers of seafloor using sonar. They detected two areas with signals that looked potentially reef-like.

The team then examined the most promising locations with an underwater drone and the Deep Sea Camera System, which functions somewhat like a set of trail cameras placed beneath the ocean.

The images revealed what appeared to be a healthy coral community.

Cameras Reveal Coral and Fish Life

Researchers observed eight different types of coral, along with eight fish species using the reef for shelter and feeding. The fish included golden African snappers, blackbar soldierfish, Guinean angelfish, West African goatfish, the Monrovia doctorfish, three-banded butterflyfish, and two species of damselfish.

Rather than forming one solid coral wall, the reef appears to consist of separate coral patches growing on rocky sections of the seabed where conditions are suitable. Scientists say additional surveys may reveal more reefs elsewhere in the surrounding area.

"To our knowledge, this is the first confirmed record of a living mesophotic coral ecosystem on the Gulf of Guinea continental shelf," said Zinzindohoué. "However, I think what we found is probably not an exception. It is more likely a reflection of how little we still know about coastal regions in West Africa and elsewhere. If we were able to find this reef again after 60 years, how many others are still undocumented or simply forgotten? So yes, I do believe there are likely more coral systems out there that we have not documented yet. But we should not assume they are everywhere. Each discovery needs to be confirmed. Without going back into the field, we are really just guessing."

How Many More Reefs Could Be Hidden?

The discovery raises the possibility that other coral ecosystems along West Africa may have been overlooked, forgotten, or never documented in the first place.

Still, the researchers caution that this is only an early look at the site. They have not yet collected physical samples of the corals, so the identifications made from the camera footage still need to be confirmed.

There is also no way yet to determine whether the corals seen in the 1960s really were dead and later recovered, or whether the original survey simply misinterpreted what was there.

Answering those questions will require much more detailed research at the site and in nearby waters.

A Possible 40 Kilometer Coral System

"This is still an initial exploration," said Zinzindohoué. "The historical reports suggested that this could be a continuous coral reef barrier extending roughly 40 kilometers parallel to the coast. We only surveyed a small section of this area, and we had a limited number of visual transects. If I had all the grant money in the world, the first thing I would do is return to the site with a proper scientific diving and sampling program. These are ecosystems that are still poorly known in this part of the world, and every additional piece of information matters.

"For me, the most exciting part is about understanding the reef's history, and what it can tell us about how the ocean in this region has changed over time. It feels like we have only just started to read an archive that has been there for a very long time."
articles.reasoning: The discovery of a living coral reef previously thought dead for over 60 years represents a significant positive environmental finding. It reveals the existence of a healthy mesophotic coral ecosystem supporting diverse marine life, suggesting overlooked biodiversity in West Africa's coastal waters. This has broad implications for marine conservation and scientific understanding of ocean ecosystems, fulfilling criteria for positive real-world impact, significance, and substance.

articles.personality_title_es: Científicos redescubren un arrecife de coral profundo vivo frente a Benín tras 60 años
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En la década de 1960, los científicos pensaban que un arrecife de coral profundo frente a Benín, en África Occidental, estaba muerto. En ese tiempo, buscaban zonas de pesca y no tenían tecnología para explorar bien las profundidades.

**Qué pasó** – Más de 60 años después, un equipo de científicos usó herramientas modernas como sonar y cámaras submarinas para mirar de nuevo. Encontraron parches de coral saludables y muchos peces viviendo en el arrecife, a más de 50 metros bajo la superficie. Este arrecife es un ecosistema coralino mesofótico, que crece en aguas más profundas y oscuras.

**Impacto** – Este hallazgo muestra que algunos arrecifes de coral que se creían muertos aún pueden estar vivos y sostener vida marina. Es la primera vez que se confirma un arrecife mesofótico vivo en esta parte del Golfo de Guinea. Esto sugiere que puede haber más arrecifes ocultos a lo largo de la costa de África Occidental que aún no conocemos.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos planean estudiar el arrecife más a fondo recolectando muestras y explorando áreas más grandes. Quieren entender cómo ha cambiado el arrecife con el tiempo y descubrir si existen otros arrecifes similares cerca. Esto ayudará a proteger estos importantes hábitats submarinos.

**Resumen en una frase** – Un arrecife de coral profundo frente a Benín, pensado muerto durante décadas, fue encontrado vivo, revelando nueva vida submarina y sugiriendo más arrecifes ocultos en África Occidental.

articles.title: CRISPR crops are coming to Europe — why bolder would be better
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 15 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02848-zFor farmers and consumers to reap the benefits, guidelines for farming gene-edited plants must be implemented with careful thought.
articles.content:
Conventional cereals and grains could be grown alongside gene-edited crops under amended EU rules.Credit: Joe Klamar/AFP via Getty

In June, the European Union overturned its strict limits on the cultivation of gene-edited crops. The change comes in the wake of growing criticism that Europe lags behind other regions when it comes to adopting innovative plant biotechnologies.

How CRISPR could yield the next blockbuster crop

Previously, all gene-edited plants were regulated as genetically modified organisms (GMOs), which sometimes incorporate DNA from other species and have raised public concern. But gene editing, using CRISPR technologies, for instance, involves only small changes to an organism’s DNA.

As a plant geneticist and agronomist, I think that the EU’s about-turn could be a game-changer for the region’s agriculture sector. But I worry that flaws in the new rules might limit their usefulness, and harm public perception of gene-edited crops.

The shift comes as climate change and geopolitical instability are putting pressure on local food security. EU pesticide bans and regulations on fertilizer use mean that there’s a need to develop crop varieties that have broad disease resistance and that use nutrients efficiently.

Gene editing can be used to instantly alter traits — such as tolerance to drought or heat — and produce crops that outperform conventional varieties. Restrictions on their use have hamstrung farmers. A 2023 impact assessment by the European Commission calculated that the annual economic loss for EU farmers could be as much as €2.7 billion (US$2.3 billion) for cereal crops by the early 2030s (see go.nature.com/4cymkvb). More-lenient rules could also help research, by stopping the brain drain and loss of intellectual property that have occurred over the past decade.

How CRISPR patent issues block Indian farmers from accessing biotech benefits

But the EU should address shortcomings in its ruling as it works on framing and communicating the new legislation.

The latest rules split gene-edited crops into two groups, called new genomic techniques 1 (NGT-1) and NGT-2 (see go.nature.com/3t3ewxt). NGT-1 crops, which can have limited alterations, are considered equivalent to plants bred through conventional means and are regulated accordingly. All other NGT plants fall under NGT-2 and remain regulated under strict GMO rules.

There are strict rules around the number of edits that NGT-1 crops can have and the number of DNA base pairs that can be changed in each edit, to align with what occurs naturally. But these constraints are arbitrary and artificial. Mutations arise randomly in nature, without limitations on type or number. What’s more, conventional breeding programmes aimed at improving several traits often involve hundreds of genetic variants.

The limits will make it hard to include several edited traits in a single crop variety, or to use gene-editing techniques to improve traits regulated by many genes, such as yield and stress resilience.

As implementation progresses, the EU should consider building in flexibility. The United States provides one example. There, crops are approved on the basis of the product rather than the breeding method used. Regulators focus on whether the characteristics of the plant pose any risks to public health or ecology, rather than on how the plant was generated and what genetic changes it has.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on the EU's policy shift to allow gene-edited crops using CRISPR, which could significantly benefit agriculture by improving crop resilience and food security amid climate change. This regulatory change has broad societal and environmental implications, potentially enabling sustainable farming and reducing economic losses. The article provides detailed context on the policy, its potential impact, and challenges, making it a substantive and meaningful positive development.
articles.personality_title: Europe opens door to gene-edited crops with new CRISPR rules
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The European Union (EU) has changed its rules about growing gene-edited crops. Until now, these crops were treated like genetically modified organisms (GMOs), which face strict limits. Gene editing, like CRISPR, only makes small changes to a plant’s DNA, different from traditional GMOs.

**What happened** – In June 2026, the EU decided to allow some gene-edited crops to be grown under new, less strict rules. These crops are split into two groups: NGT-1, which have small changes and are treated like normal plants, and NGT-2, which still face tight GMO rules. The goal is to help farmers grow crops that can better resist drought, heat, and diseases.

**Impact** – This change could help European farmers save billions of euros by growing stronger crops that use nutrients better and survive tough weather. It also helps scientists keep working on new plant varieties in Europe instead of losing ideas to other countries. However, the current rules limit how many changes can be made in one crop, which might slow progress on improving important traits like yield and stress resistance.

**What's next step** – The EU will need to update and explain these rules carefully to make sure farmers and the public understand and trust gene-edited crops. They might also look at how other countries, like the United States, approve crops based on safety, not just how they are made. This could lead to more flexible rules that allow better crops in the future.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The EU’s new rules for gene-edited crops mark a hopeful step toward stronger, more resilient farming but will need careful updates to unlock their full potential.
articles.personality_title_fr: L’Europe ouvre la porte aux cultures modifiées par CRISPR avec de nouvelles règles
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – L’Union européenne (UE) a modifié ses règles concernant la culture des plantes modifiées par édition génétique. Jusqu’à présent, ces plantes étaient traitées comme des organismes génétiquement modifiés (OGM), soumis à de fortes restrictions. L’édition génétique, comme CRISPR, ne fait que de petits changements dans l’ADN d’une plante, ce qui est différent des OGM classiques.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – En juin 2026, l’UE a décidé d’autoriser certaines plantes modifiées par édition génétique à être cultivées sous des règles moins strictes. Ces plantes sont divisées en deux groupes : NGT-1, avec de petits changements et traitées comme des plantes normales, et NGT-2, qui restent soumises aux règles strictes des OGM. L’objectif est d’aider les agriculteurs à cultiver des plantes plus résistantes à la sécheresse, à la chaleur et aux maladies.

**Impact** – Ce changement pourrait aider les agriculteurs européens à économiser des milliards d’euros en cultivant des plantes plus fortes, qui utilisent mieux les nutriments et résistent aux conditions difficiles. Cela aide aussi les chercheurs à continuer leurs travaux en Europe plutôt que de perdre leurs idées au profit d’autres pays. Cependant, les règles actuelles limitent le nombre de modifications possibles dans une plante, ce qui pourrait ralentir les progrès sur des traits importants comme le rendement et la résistance au stress.

**Prochaine étape** – L’UE devra mettre à jour et expliquer ces règles avec soin pour que les agriculteurs et le public comprennent et fassent confiance aux plantes modifiées par édition génétique. Elle pourrait aussi s’inspirer d’autres pays, comme les États-Unis, qui approuvent les plantes selon leur sécurité, et non seulement selon leur méthode de création. Cela pourrait conduire à des règles plus flexibles pour de meilleures plantes à l’avenir.

**Une phrase clé** – Les nouvelles règles de l’UE sur les plantes modifiées par édition génétique sont un pas prometteur vers une agriculture plus forte et plus résistante, mais elles devront être ajustées pour atteindre leur plein potentiel.
articles.personality_title_es: Europa abre la puerta a cultivos editados con CRISPR con nuevas reglas
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La Unión Europea (UE) ha cambiado sus reglas sobre el cultivo de plantas editadas genéticamente. Hasta ahora, estas plantas se trataban como organismos modificados genéticamente (OMG), que tienen muchas restricciones. La edición genética, como CRISPR, solo hace pequeños cambios en el ADN de una planta, diferente de los OMG tradicionales.

**Qué pasó** – En junio de 2026, la UE decidió permitir que algunos cultivos editados genéticamente se cultiven con reglas menos estrictas. Estas plantas se dividen en dos grupos: NGT-1, que tienen cambios pequeños y se tratan como plantas normales, y NGT-2, que siguen bajo reglas estrictas de OMG. El objetivo es ayudar a los agricultores a cultivar plantas que resistan mejor la sequía, el calor y las enfermedades.

**Impacto** – Este cambio podría ayudar a los agricultores europeos a ahorrar miles de millones de euros al cultivar plantas más fuertes que usan mejor los nutrientes y sobreviven a condiciones difíciles. También ayuda a los científicos a seguir investigando en Europa en lugar de perder ideas frente a otros países. Sin embargo, las reglas actuales limitan cuántos cambios puede tener una planta, lo que podría frenar la mejora de rasgos importantes como el rendimiento y la resistencia al estrés.

**Próximo paso** – La UE tendrá que actualizar y explicar bien estas reglas para que los agricultores y el público entiendan y confíen en los cultivos editados genéticamente. También podrían mirar cómo otros países, como Estados Unidos, aprueban cultivos basándose en su seguridad, no solo en cómo se hicieron. Esto podría llevar a reglas más flexibles para mejores cultivos en el futuro.

**Una frase clave** – Las nuevas reglas de la UE para cultivos editados genéticamente son un paso esperanzador hacia una agricultura más fuerte y resistente, pero necesitarán ajustes para alcanzar todo su potencial.
